fatal_errors: The proposed thermomechanically induced amorphous/nanocrystalline surface layer is unrelated to the target comparison between as-printed and precipitation-aged Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
It omits the governing Cr2O3-scale mechanism, Cr depletion in L12/L21 precipitate regions, and precipitate–matrix interfaces as oxygen short-circuit paths.

The cited study concerns friction and wear in ultra-high vacuum, where oxidation was deliberately mitigated; it provides no support for improved high-temperature oxidation resistance or self-healing oxide formation.

The assertion that a high density of grain boundaries blocks oxygen diffusion is unsupported and conflicts with the common role of boundaries as rapid diffusion paths, as well as with the target mechanism.
The predicted improvement after processing has the wrong direction relative to the target result, in which aged material consistently oxidized more than the as-printed baseline.
explanation: The response addresses the broad topic of oxidation resistance in an MPEA and proposes a nominally controlled treated-versus-untreated experiment, but it does not reconstruct the relevant alloy, precipitation-aging intervention, oxide architecture, or measured behavior. Its 600–900 °C range only partially overlaps the target's 600–1200 °C, up-to-96-hour exposures, and it lacks time-resolved mass-gain kinetics, power-law analysis, oxide-thickness kinetics, and activation-energy comparison. The experiment could test its own speculative hypothesis, although thermomechanical processing introduces confounders and the falsification rule is generic. Most importantly, the sole evidence is a wear study conducted under conditions designed to suppress oxidation, so the extrapolation to oxygen-barrier and self-healing behavior is not evidence-valid. The idea is comparatively novel but remains unsupported rather than a plausible evidence-based alternative.
